[/page/1/Text/18] The therapist's training was behaviorally oriented, and he was experienced in behavior therapy.

[/page/4/Text/11] No significant differences were found between the group means of the cognitive-behavioral and relaxation conditions nor between the cognitive-behavioral and wait-list conditions.

[/page/4/Text/14] The ANCOVA at posttreatment yielded significant differences between groups, F(2, 20) = 5.33 \ p < .05. Comparisons indicated that the relaxation training group (Q_p = 3.95, p < .05) and cognitive-behavioral group (Q_p = 3.61, p < .05) means were significantly higher than the wait-list group mean.
[/page/5/Text/7] This study found both cognitive-behavioral therapy and relaxation training to be effective in the treatment of moderately depressed adolescents.

To qualify for inclusion in the study, students were required to satisfy all of the following criteria: (a) a BDI score of 12 or greater; (b) a RADS score of 72 or greater; (c) a BID score of 20 or greater; (d) no current use of medication or other treatment for depression or related disorders; and (e) willingness to participate in a treatment program.

[/page/1/Text/14] At pretest, the mean BDI depression score for the 30 subjects was 18.23; according to Beck's classification scheme, subjects were manifesting a moderate level of clinical depression.

[/page/3/Text/7] In general, subjects presented moderate to severe levels of depression based on BDI, RADS, and BID scores. [/page/3/Text/9] Thirty depressed adolescents were accepted for inclusion in the study

The text discusses self-concept measures and improved general self-esteem, but does not mention any diagnostic criteria for depression or any other disorder for inclusion or exclusion.

[/page/5/Text/14] It is important to note that subjects in this study were not formally diagnosed as having major depression according to the DSM-III or Research Diagnostic Criteria (Spitzer, Endicott, & Robins, 1978).

evidence.quote: [/page/0/Text/5] Outcome measures included self-report and clinical interviews for depression as well as measures of self-esteem and anxiety.
Students were asked by their teachers to complete preassembled packets of questionnaires. ... The BID was administered by the second author who also served as therapist.

[page/1/Text/20] Two self-report measures and a structured clinical interview were used to measure treatment outcome. The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES; Rosenberg, 1965), a measure of general self-concept, consists of 10 items and uses a 4-point Likert-type response format. A high score reflects a high level of self-esteem. The high school version of the Academic Self-Concept Scale (ASCS-HS; Reynolds, 1981) is a downward extension of the standard form of the ASCS developed by Reynolds, Ramirez, Magrina, and Allen (1980) and consists of 15 items.; [page/2/Text/7] Anxiety. From the interview tapes, the rater was unable to distinguish the condition to which each subject had been assigned.
